name: Imhotep
date_note: fl.; reign of Djoser (3rd Dynasty), approximate
making_significance: Later Egyptian tradition credits the official Imhotep with designing the Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, the earliest large cut-stone monument in Egypt.
defined_by: Egyptian tradition (Manetho); Egyptologists, from his name on a Djoser statue base
leaves_out: the quarrymen, masons and rotating labour gangs who built the complex
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: His name and titles on a Djoser statue base are contemporary; the architect role is later tradition; he was later deified. links: DYN002; POL001

name: Irtysen
date_note: fl.; reign of Mentuhotep II (11th Dynasty), approximate
making_significance: His funerary stela (Louvre C 14) is a rare Egyptian text in which a craftsman describes his own skills in carving and in preparing materials, which he says he taught only to his eldest son.
leaves_out: the workshop whose methods were kept within the family; the labourers who quarried and moved stone
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Translations of the technical passage differ; check against the Louvre record. links: DYN003

name: Senenmut
date_note: fl.; under Hatshepsut, death date unknown
making_significance: The steward of Hatshepsut is associated with the design of her temple at Deir el-Bahari and appears in unusual block statues holding the princess Neferure.
leaves_out: the builders and quarry labourers; the uncertainty over how much he himself designed
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Architect attribution is inferred from titles and proximity. links: DYN004

name: Hatshepsut
making_significance: As king she commissioned the temple at Deir el-Bahari, obelisks at Karnak and an expedition to Punt whose return with incense trees is carved in her temple reliefs.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: the builders and voyagers; the people of Punt shown in the reliefs
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: The Met holds many statues from Deir el-Bahari. links: DYN004; POL001

name: Thutmose (sculptor)
making_significance: Excavators identified a house and workshop at Amarna as his from an inscribed fragment; it held plaster studies and the painted bust of Nefertiti.
leaves_out: the assistants whose plaster and stone studies were found in the workshop
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Identification rests on an ivory horse blinker naming a sculptor Thutmose; the bust is in Berlin and Egypt has asked for its return. links: STY082

name: Sennedjem
date_note: fl.; reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II, approximate
making_significance: A workman of the royal tomb-builders' village, his painted tomb (TT1) and its coffins and furniture show what the royal craftsmen made for their own families.
defined_by: Egyptologists (tomb found intact in 1886); his own titles ("Servant in the Place of Truth")
leaves_out: his wife Iyneferti and relatives shown in the tomb; the fellow workmen who helped cut and paint it
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Verified round 2: the Met holds about 29 items from TT1, including the coffin sets of Iyneferti and of Khonsu; Sennedjem's own coffin set and sarcophagus are in Cairo (National Museum of Egyptian Civilization). links: MKR090

name: Amanishakheto
date_note: fl.; late 1st century BCE to early 1st century CE, approximate
making_significance: The Meroitic queen's pyramid at Meroe held gold jewellery that Giuseppe Ferlini found when he pulled down its top in 1834; the pieces are now in Munich and Berlin.
leaves_out: the Meroitic goldsmiths; Sudanese claims to objects now held abroad
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Reign dates uncertain; parts of Ferlini's account are doubted. links: POL003

name: Giuseppe Ferlini
making_significance: The Italian physician and treasure hunter pulled down pyramids at Meroe in 1834 and sold the gold he found to the royal collections in Munich and Berlin.
leaves_out: the Meroitic makers and the people buried there; Sudanese claims to the objects
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Treated as looting in current scholarship. links: POL003

name: Gebre Mesqel Lalibela
making_significance: Ethiopian tradition credits the Zagwe king with ordering the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, though archaeologists date parts of the complex earlier.
leaves_out: the stone-cutters, whose names do not survive; builders of the earlier parts of the complex
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: The churches are active places of worship. links: DYN033

name: Zara Yaqob
making_significance: The Solomonic emperor promoted devotion to Mary, which increased demand for painted Marian icons and illuminated books of the Miracles of Mary.
leaves_out: the monastic painters, among them Fre Seyon, and the scribes
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Walters Art Museum (CC0)

name: Fre Seyon
making_significance: The monk-painter is the earliest named Ethiopian painter to whom surviving icons of Mary and Child are attributed, working in the reign of Zara Yaqob.
defined_by: art historians (Marilyn Heldman), from inscriptions naming him
leaves_out: workshop assistants and unnamed monastic painters
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Attributions rest on a few inscribed icons.

name: Tewodros II
making_significance: The emperor gathered manuscripts, crowns and church objects at Maqdala, which British forces took after his death in 1868; hundreds of manuscripts went to British libraries and museums.
leaves_out: the scribes and craftsmen whose work he gathered; the Ethiopian Church's claim to the tabotat
free_sources: British Library digitised manuscripts (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Tabotat must not be displayed. links: POL007

name: Richard Rivington Holmes
making_significance: The British Museum's representative on the 1868 Maqdala expedition bought looted manuscripts and objects at the army's prize auction for British collections.
leaves_out: the Ethiopian makers and owners; the soldiers' looting that came before the auction
free_sources: British Museum Collection Online (CC BY-NC-SA, link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Olowe of Ise
making_significance: The Yorùbá carver made palace doors, veranda posts and lidded bowls for Ekiti rulers; a door he carved for the Ogoga of Ikere went to the British Empire Exhibition in 1924 and then to the British Museum.
defined_by: Yorùbá oral praise (oriki); art historians (Roslyn Walker)
leaves_out: the assistants who roughed out his work; the exchange by which the Ikere door left Nigeria
free_sources: British Museum Collection Online (CC BY-NC-SA, link out);Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only (works in copyright)
notes: Useful for attribution: named by praise poetry, not signature. links: EVT012

name: Areogun
making_significance: The Yorùbá carver from Osi-Ilorin made Epa masks, doors and figures for shrines and palaces, and later also for church and colonial patrons.
leaves_out: his workshop, including his son George Bandele
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Lamidi Olonade Fakeye
making_significance: The Yorùbá carver trained at the Oye-Ekiti Catholic workshop and made doors and figures for churches, universities and collectors, carrying an Ekiti carving lineage into modern institutions.
leaves_out: his teacher George Bandele and the lineage workshop
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright);Wikimedia Commons

name: Esigie
making_significance: Benin tradition links the Oba's reign to brass plaques, ivory pendant masks made for his mother Idia and early trade with the Portuguese that brought brass in quantity.
leaves_out: the Igun Eronmwon casters and Igbesanmwan carvers who made the works
free_sources: Digital Benin (licence per lending museum);Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum Collection Online (CC BY-NC-SA, link out);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Dating plaques to his reign is debated. links: DYN038; POL026; MKR001; MKR002

name: Idia
making_significance: The first Iyoba (Queen Mother) of Benin is associated with ivory pendant masks worn at court, several of which were taken in 1897.
leaves_out: the ivory carvers; the women of the court beyond royal title-holders
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum Collection Online (CC BY-NC-SA, link out);Digital Benin (licence per lending museum);Wikimedia Commons
notes: The masks' identification with Idia is traditional. links: MKR002

name: Ovonramwen Nogbaisi
making_significance: The Oba reigned when British forces took Benin City in 1897 and removed thousands of court objects; he died in exile in Calabar.
leaves_out: the guild casters and carvers whose work was taken
free_sources: Digital Benin (licence per lending museum);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ewuare II
making_significance: The present Oba is a leading claimant for the return of Benin works taken in 1897 and the head of the court under which the casting and carving guilds still work.
leaves_out: the guild members; other Nigerian bodies in disputes over custody
free_sources: Digital Benin (licence per lending museum);community-published site (link-out)
notes: Custody of returned objects has been disputed between the palace and state bodies. links: INS082

name: Harry Rawson
making_significance: The British admiral commanded the 1897 punitive expedition that burned Benin City and removed its brass and ivory works, many later auctioned in London.
leaves_out: the Benin guild makers; the people killed in the attack
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Felix von Luschan
making_significance: The Berlin museum curator acquired hundreds of Benin works after 1897 and published Die Altertümer von Benin (1919), building one of the largest holdings.
leaves_out: the Benin makers; the soldiers and dealers who supplied him
free_sources: Digital Benin (licence per lending museum);Internet Archive (public-domain scans)
notes: He also collected human remains; that collection raises further issues.

name: Augustus Pitt Rivers
other_names: Augustus Henry Lane Fox Pitt Rivers
making_significance: The army officer and collector arranged objects in typological series meant to show technical evolution and gave his collection to Oxford in 1884.
leaves_out: the makers of the objects; the people from whom Benin and other works were taken
free_sources: Pitt Rivers Museum Collections Online (link out);Wikimedia Commons
notes: He bought Benin works after 1897 for his second, private museum at Farnham. links: INS053

name: Mansa Musa
making_significance: The Mali ruler's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 spent so much gold in Cairo that chroniclers noted its effect, and tradition says he brought the poet-architect al-Sahili back with him.
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;ritual and belief
leaves_out: the gold miners of Bambuk and Bure; the enslaved people who travelled in his caravan
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Abu Ishaq al-Sahili
date_note: born c. 1290 in Granada; died 1346 in Timbuktu
making_significance: The Andalusi poet is credited by tradition with designing a palace and the Djinguereber mosque for Mansa Musa, though the earthen building tradition he worked in was local.
defined_by: Ibn Battuta and Ibn Khaldun; later tradition
leaves_out: the local masons who built and maintain the mosques
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Attribution is traditional and debated. links: POL036

name: Ismaila Traoré
making_significance: As head of the Djenné masons' guild he led the rebuilding of the Great Mosque of Djenné, completed in 1907.
defined_by: Djenné oral tradition; French colonial records
leaves_out: the masons' guild and the townspeople who replaster the mosque each year
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Abdel Kader Haidara
date_note: fl.; took charge of his family library in 1981; birth year not verified; living
making_significance: The Timbuktu librarian organised the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of manuscripts to Bamako in 2012–13 to protect them from occupying armed groups.
leaves_out: the families who own the manuscripts and the couriers who carried them
free_sources: community-published site (link-out)
notes: Figures for manuscripts moved vary (about 350,000–377,000). links: MKR010

name: Osei Tutu
making_significance: The founder of the Asante state is linked by tradition with the Golden Stool, the sacred seat of the nation, and with the rise of Kumasi's goldsmith and weaving crafts.
leaves_out: the priest Okomfo Anokye whom tradition credits with bringing the Stool; the goldsmiths
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: The Golden Stool is not displayed; do not illustrate. links: POL029; DYN039

name: Njoya
making_significance: The Bamum king created the Bamum script, ran royal workshops for brass casting, beadwork and weaving at Foumban and designed a new palace.
defined_by: Bamum court; German and French colonial records
leaves_out: the palace artisans and scribes; the women of the court who did much of the beadwork
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: His beaded throne was given to Kaiser Wilhelm II in 1908 (now Berlin). links: MKR004; POL025

name: Emil Torday
making_significance: The Hungarian ethnographer collected thousands of Kuba and other Congo objects for the British Museum in 1907–09, including ndop figures.
leaves_out: the Kuba makers; the colonial conditions of acquisition
free_sources: British Museum Collection Online (CC BY-NC-SA, link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Leo Frobenius
making_significance: The German ethnologist removed objects from Ife in 1910 and built theories of African culture circles from collections gathered on his expeditions.
leaves_out: the Ife people and court from whom works were taken; his African assistants
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: The Olokun head he acquired was seized by the colonial authorities; the one in Ife may be a later copy. links: CIV011

name: Ladi Kwali
date_note: born c. 1925; joined the Abuja Pottery Training Centre (founded 1952; 1951 is Cardew's appointment) in December 1954
making_significance: The Gbari potter from Kwali made hand-built water pots and then, at the Abuja Pottery Training Centre, glazed stoneware that was shown in London (Berkeley Galleries, 1958–62), Paris and Washington.
leaves_out: the Gbari women potters, including her aunt, from whom she learned
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Pictured on the Nigerian 20 naira note. links: INS122

name: Michael Cardew
making_significance: The English potter ran the Abuja Pottery Training Centre in northern Nigeria from 1951, after working at Vumë in Ghana, joining Leach-style stoneware to local potters' skills.
leaves_out: the Nigerian and Ghanaian potters at Abuja and Vumë, few of whom are named
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright);Wikimedia Commons

name: Uche Okeke
making_significance: The Nigerian artist adapted Igbo uli body and wall designs, traditionally painted by women, into modern drawing and painting and taught this approach at Nsukka.
leaves_out: the Igbo women uli painters whose motifs he adapted
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Ben Enwonwu
making_significance: The Nigerian sculptor and painter, son of an Igbo carver, made public sculptures such as Anyanwu (1955) and had an early international career.
leaves_out: his father's carving practice; the Onitsha masquerade makers whose forms he painted
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: El Anatsui
making_significance: The Ghanaian artist, long based at Nsukka, joins flattened bottle caps and foil seals with copper wire into large hangings that recall kente cloth and trade histories.
leaves_out: the studio assistants who cut, fold and join the caps
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Demas Nwoko
making_significance: The Nigerian artist and architect built the Dominican Chapel in Ibadan and his New Culture Studio, using local materials and forms shaped by climate.
leaves_out: the builders and craftsmen who worked on his buildings
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Ibrahim El-Salahi
making_significance: The Sudanese painter drew on Arabic calligraphy and Sudanese decorative forms to help found the modernism of the Khartoum School.
leaves_out: the calligraphers and craft makers whose forms he adapted
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Kamala Ibrahim Ishaq
making_significance: The Sudanese painter co-founded the Crystalist group in 1976 and drew on women's zar spirit-possession gatherings in her work.
leaves_out: the women of the zar gatherings she painted
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Chaibia Tallal
making_significance: The self-taught Moroccan painter began in the 1960s and was exhibited in Europe, where critics framed her work as 'naive' or art brut, a label later questioned.
leaves_out: the rural colour and textile traditions she drew on
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)
notes: Check the critic credited with her 1966 debut.

name: Farid Belkahia
making_significance: The Casablanca School artist worked on hammered copper and on lambskin coloured with henna, taking materials and signs from Amazigh and urban crafts.
leaves_out: the tanners, dyers and coppersmiths of Marrakech who prepared his materials
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Mohamed Melehi
making_significance: The Moroccan painter and designer of the Casablanca School made hard-edge wave paintings and covers for the review Souffles, and brought Amazigh crafts into art teaching.
leaves_out: fellow teachers Farid Belkahia, Toni Maraini and Bert Flint; the artisans whose work entered the syllabus
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Hassan Fathy
making_significance: The Egyptian architect built New Gourna (from 1946) in mud brick with Nubian vault-building masons and argued for local building in Architecture for the Poor.
defined_by: himself (Gourna: A Tale of Two Villages, 1969)
leaves_out: the Nubian masons whose vaulting technique he used; the Gourna residents who resisted being moved
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Ramses Wissa Wassef
making_significance: The Egyptian architect founded a tapestry workshop at Harrania in 1952 where village children learned to weave their own designs directly on the loom without cartoons.
leaves_out: his wife Sophie Habib Gorgy, who continued the centre; the weavers themselves
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Susanne Wenger
making_significance: The Austrian artist, who became an Osun priestess, worked with Yorùbá builders and sculptors of the New Sacred Art group to rebuild shrines in the Osun-Osogbo grove.
leaves_out: the Nigerian artists of the New Sacred Art group, such as Adebisi Akanji
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: The grove is a World Heritage site and active shrine.

name: Ulli Beier
making_significance: The German editor co-founded the Mbari Club in Ibadan and the journal Black Orpheus and backed the Oshogbo workshops, shaping how Nigerian modern art reached foreign audiences; he later worked in Papua New Guinea.
leaves_out: Georgina Beier, who ran workshops; the Nigerian co-founders of Mbari
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Nike Davies-Okundaye
making_significance: The Yorùbá textile artist teaches adire indigo resist-dyeing through art centres in Osogbo, Lagos and elsewhere, keeping a women's craft in active training.
leaves_out: the women dyers of Osogbo from whom she learned
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Esther Mahlangu
making_significance: The Ndebele painter carried women's homestead-painting designs onto canvas and objects, including a BMW Art Car in 1991.
leaves_out: the Ndebele women who paint homesteads without public credit
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Noria Mabasa
making_significance: The Venda artist worked first in clay and then in wood, a medium locally reserved for men, making large carved figures.
leaves_out: the women potters whose practice she began in
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Nesta Nala
making_significance: The Zulu potter made burnished beer vessels (izinkamba) with raised amasumpa patterns and trained her daughters in the craft.
leaves_out: the women potters who taught her, including her mother
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Bonnie Ntshalintshali
making_significance: The Ardmore ceramicist made painted figurative sculptures of biblical and everyday scenes.
leaves_out: Fée Halsted, who founded Ardmore, and the other Ardmore artists
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Kane Kwei
making_significance: The Ga carpenter from Teshie is credited with popularising figurative coffins shaped as objects linked to the dead person's life.
leaves_out: other carpenters making such coffins, such as Ataa Oko; his apprentices, including Paa Joe
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)
notes: Who first made such coffins is disputed. links: STY179

name: Edward Saidi Tingatinga
making_significance: The Tanzanian painter began painting with enamel house paint on ceiling board in Dar es Salaam around 1968, founding a style continued by a cooperative.
leaves_out: the relatives and apprentices who continued the style
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Chéri Samba
making_significance: The Kinshasa painter started as a sign painter and made text-and-image paintings central to Congolese popular painting.
leaves_out: the sign-painting workshops and fellow popular painters
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Papa Ibra Tall
making_significance: The Senegalese artist directed the tapestry workshop at Thiès from 1966, turning paintings of the École de Dakar into woven hangings.
leaves_out: the weavers of Thiès who wove the tapestries
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Léopold Sédar Senghor
making_significance: As Senegal's first president he funded the École de Dakar, the Thiès tapestry works and the 1966 World Festival of Negro Arts as state cultural policy.
leaves_out: artists working outside the Negritude style the state favoured
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Felwine Sarr
making_significance: The Senegalese economist co-wrote with Bénédicte Savoy the 2018 report to the French president that recommended returning African objects taken in the colonial period.
leaves_out: the communities of origin consulted unevenly; museum staff in Africa
free_sources: open-access report or journal article (link out)

name: Bénédicte Savoy
making_significance: The French art historian co-wrote the 2018 restitution report and has written on the history of European museums' demands for and refusals of returns.
leaves_out: earlier African restitution claims and claimants, such as those of the 1970s
free_sources: open-access report or journal article (link out)

name: Nana Oforiatta Ayim
date_note: fl.; curated Ghana's first Venice Biennale pavilion in 2019; birth year not verified; living
making_significance: The Ghanaian writer and art historian curated Ghana's first Venice Biennale pavilion (2019) and leads a pan-African cultural encyclopaedia project.
leaves_out: the makers and archivists documented by the encyclopaedia
free_sources: community-published site (link-out)
notes: Birth year could not be verified from a reliable source in the round-2 check, so a floruit is given.

name: Ranavalona I
making_significance: The Merina queen used forced labour (fanompoana) to build Jean Laborde's foundries and workshops at Mantasoa, which made guns, glass, soap and textiles.
leaves_out: the forced labourers at Mantasoa, many of whom died
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Jean Laborde
making_significance: The French adventurer built an industrial complex at Mantasoa for Ranavalona I, casting cannon and making glass, soap and silk with thousands of forced labourers.
leaves_out: the forced labourers who did the work
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Tippu Tip
making_significance: The Zanzibari trader ran caravans into the Congo basin that moved ivory to the coast for Indian, European and American workshops, using enslaved porters and trading enslaved people.
leaves_out: the enslaved porters and captives; the elephant hunters
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Ghezo
making_significance: The Dahomey king's reign saw court appliqué cloths and brass works expand, funded in part by the Atlantic trade in enslaved people.
leaves_out: the enslaved people sold; the Yemadje and other court artisans
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Béhanzin
making_significance: The last independent king of Dahomey's palace works, including royal statues, were taken by French forces in 1892; 26 of them were returned to Benin in 2021.
leaves_out: the court artists who carved the royal statues, such as Sosa Adede
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Attributions of the royal statues to named carvers need checking. links: POL030

name: Ibn Khaldun
making_significance: The North African historian's Muqaddimah (1377) treats crafts as a product of settled urban life and explains their decline with the decline of cities.
leaves_out: rural and nomadic makers whom his model ranked below urban crafts
free_sources: Internet Archive (public-domain scans);Wikimedia Commons

name: Muhammad Ali Pasha
making_significance: The governor of Egypt set up state factories for cotton spinning and weaving, arms and shipbuilding from the 1810s, staffed largely with conscripted workers.
leaves_out: the conscripted workers and the peasants forced to grow cotton
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Amina of Zazzau
date_note: fl.; dates disputed: often given as reign c. 1576–1610 (16th century), but the Kano Chronicle makes her a contemporary of Muhammad Dauda (r. 1421–38)
making_significance: Hausa tradition credits the queen of Zazzau with fortifying towns with earthen walls (ganuwar Amina).
defined_by: Hausa oral tradition; the Kano Chronicle
leaves_out: the labourers and later rulers who built and kept the walls
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Historicity is debated; written accounts are late. links: POL032

name: Reinata Sadimba
making_significance: The Makonde artist makes figurative ceramic sculptures, extending a pot-making practice associated with Makonde women.
leaves_out: the Makonde women potters from whom she learned
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Magdalene Odundo
making_significance: The Kenyan-born potter, based in Britain, makes hand-built burnished vessels fired to black and orange, drawing on potters she studied in Nigeria and Kenya.
leaves_out: the Gbari and other potters she learned from, including at Abuja
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: Margaret Trowell
making_significance: The British teacher started art classes at Makerere in Kampala in 1937 that became East Africa's leading art school.
leaves_out: the Ugandan students and teachers who shaped the school
free_sources: collection search link-out only (works in copyright)

name: K'inich Janaab Pakal
making_significance: The Palenque king commissioned the Temple of the Inscriptions, whose tomb held his jade mosaic mask and a carved sarcophagus lid.
leaves_out: the sculptors and stucco workers of Palenque
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Lady Six Sky
making_significance: The noblewoman from Dos Pilas held power at Naranjo and is shown on stelae she commissioned standing over a captive.
leaves_out: the sculptors of the Naranjo stelae; the captives shown
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Her exact title and role are debated. links: CIV018

name: Aj Maxam
date_note: fl.; mid-to-late 8th century (Art Institute of Chicago); his father acceded at Naranjo in 765 and one study puts his birth in the 770s, so activity may run to c. 800
making_significance: A painter-scribe of Naranjo, son of a Naranjo king and a noblewoman from Yaxha, signed polychrome drinking vessels, showing that elite Maya painters could be named.
leaves_out: the potters who formed the vessels he painted
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Verified round 2: the Water-Lily Vessel inscription names him, his royal Naranjo lineage and his parents; his mother was a lady of Yaxha. links: MKR021

name: Moctezuma II
making_significance: The Mexica ruler kept featherworkers, goldsmiths and lapidaries whose work reached Europe through Cortés; a feather headdress in Vienna was later linked to him by tradition.
leaves_out: the amanteca featherworkers and other artisans who made the objects
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Digital Florentine Codex, Getty Research Institute (link out)
notes: The Vienna headdress's link to him is not proven; Mexico has asked for its return. links: POL051; MKR019

name: Diego de Alvarado Huanitzin
making_significance: The Nahua governor of Mexico-Tenochtitlan sent the feather mosaic Mass of Saint Gregory (1539) to Pope Paul III, the earliest dated colonial featherwork.
defined_by: inscription on the work; art historians
leaves_out: the amanteca featherworkers who made it
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: The work is in the Musée des Jacobins, Auch. links: MKR019

name: Bernardino de Sahagún
making_significance: The Franciscan friar directed the Florentine Codex (completed c. 1577), in which Nahua scholars and painters recorded crafts such as featherwork, goldsmithing and lapidary work.
leaves_out: the Nahua scholars (Antonio Valeriano, Martín Jacobita, Pedro de San Buenaventura, Alonso Vegerano, Diego de Grado, Bonifacio Maximiliano, Mateo Severino), the painters and the elders they interviewed
free_sources: Digital Florentine Codex, Getty Research Institute (link out);Wikimedia Commons

name: Martín de la Cruz
making_significance: A Nahua physician at Tlatelolco wrote the illustrated herbal known as the Libellus de Medicinalibus Indorum Herbis (1552), translated into Latin by Juan Badiano.
leaves_out: the unnamed painters of the plant images; the translator Juan Badiano
